source.title: Neural Approximators for Low-Thrust Trajectory Transfer Cost and Reachability

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how neural-network loss changes with model and dataset size in low-thrust trajectory approximation, a new application area. It does not test language-model pretraining loss or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports low-thrust model- and dataset-size scaling results in Figures 1–2 and architecture-specific test losses in Tables 5–6. These are not language-model pretraining results, so they do not test the listed versions as worded. The paper also cites the original language-model scaling work; cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper explicitly checks whether the scaling law holds outside language models. It sweeps MLP size (about 10^2–10^5 parameters) and dataset size (10^5–10^8 samples) for low-thrust trajectory regression. It reports test loss falling roughly linearly on log-log axes (Fig. 1, Fig. 2; Tables 5–6). That bears on V5, the power-law form in another domain and training regime. The other versions are language-model-specific or are not examined.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that an approximate scaling law holds for low-thrust trajectory approximation, that larger models and datasets improve test loss, and that this justifies generating over 100 million samples. They add that model size is capped by inference-time limits.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses low-thrust trajectory regression, sweeps neural-network architecture and dataset scale, and reports task-specific test losses. It does not use language-model pretraining, language-model token/compute sweeps, or compute-optimal allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that architecture and dataset size affect performance. It also states that learning rate has the greatest effect among the tuned hyperparameters, weight-decay ratio has comparatively minor influence, smaller batch sizes generally perform better, and poor choices such as an excessively large learning rate can degrade performance by orders of magnitude.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report that scaling in model size and dataset size is independent: increasing dataset size does not change the best model size, and vice versa. No numbers are given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In low-thrust trajectory regression, the best model size is insensitive to dataset size.

fits_no_version.finding: Hyperparameters strongly modulate loss at fixed architecture (9×128). A poor learning rate degrades loss by up to orders of magnitude, and smaller batches give lower loss (Tables 7–8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hyperparameter choice can dominate scale effects in small-MLP regression.

record.problems: The scaling plots do not provide exact numerical loss values in the text; the model-size trend is described as approximate. For architecture sweeps, only the best result after tuning other hyperparameters is reported. The scaling experiments use a 100,000-sample dataset, and do not test language-model pretraining or compute-optimal allocation.
record.rows_left_out: None of the reported model-size or dataset-size scaling results were left out. Other input-representation and hyperparameter comparisons were not included because they do not report model- or dataset-scale effects relevant to the claim.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss; compute as a scaling variable.
No fitted law is used to predict a larger run. The 100M-sample run is motivated by the trend, but its loss is not compared with any extrapolation.
Compute-optimal allocation is not studied. Only an informal remark that model and data scaling are independent.
Shape effects at fixed parameter count in language models are not tested.
Exponent values and the exact power-law form (no fit); compute scaling; other modalities such as image and video; repeated data; fine-tuning and transfer.
Downstream tasks versus scale. The third-party validation compares only against a reference model, not across scales.
Fitting-choice dependence of exponents is not examined.

missing.what: The model size held fixed during the dataset-size sweep, and readable loss values from Fig. 2 (endpoints roughly 10^0 to 10^-2)
missing.locator: Figure 2 and the Scaling Law subsection

missing.what: Parameter counts for each layer×neuron configuration, needed to place Tables 5–6 on the Fig. 1 x-axis

record.verdict_notes: The paper is not an original source. Its evidence is qualitative: points read off log-log figures, no fitted exponents, no compute axis, and the model-size sweep uses only 100k samples. The rows were re-linked from 'none' to V5, because V5 explicitly covers other domains and training regimes. The individual grid-cell rows are meaningful only as a group.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger language-model runs from fits on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, including its trend with compute.
Architecture effects on language-model loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes as specified, such as image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream-task predictability from model scale or pretraining loss.
Setup- or fitting-dependent language-model exponents, compute-optimal splits, or systematic departures from single power laws.

rows.subject: ∆v model
rows.operation_detail: Test loss for a network architecture in the architecture sweep
rows.note: Each architecture is fine-tuned over other hyperparameters; only the best result is reported.
rows.check: Each row is one cell of the ∆v layer×neuron grid with no baseline, so a single row cannot show scaling. Read as a group, they show the model-size trend behind Fig. 1. ∆v test loss falls with width at depth ≥3, e.g. 9 layers: 0.070 (8 neurons) to 0.003 (128 neurons). The 8-neuron column barely moves with depth (0.072–0.070), and the 128-neuron column plateaus at 0.003. Parameter counts are not stated and must be computed from width and depth. Each architecture is the best over a hyperparameter sweep on a 100k-sample dataset.
